question: He said a number of lies and then went without saying me good bye.
options: He said a number of lies
correctAnswer: He said a number of lies
explanation: Use 'told' in place of 'said'.

question: Not only we saw the Education Minister but also the Chief Minister.
explanation: Place 'not only' after 'saw'.

question: I came directly to my residence from the airport.
explanation: Say 'direct'.

question: I signed on the receipt in the morning but the pay has not been disbursed to me.
options: in the morning but the pay
has not been disbursed to me.
explanation: Drop 'on' after 'signed'.

question: This is the same story which I heard from him yesterday.
explanation: Use 'that' in place of 'which'.

question: What to speak of food even water was not available.
explanation: Use 'Not to speak of' in place of 'What to speak of'.

question: It was difficult to get out because the street was full of people from one end to another.
options: It was difficult to get out
because the street was full of people
explanation: Say 'one end to other'.

question: It has been our custom from time immemorial to be hospitable to those who come to our doors.
options: hospitable to those who come to our doors.
correctAnswer: hospitable to those who come to our doors.
explanation: Say 'door'.

question: She does not hardly know what happened yesterday.
explanation: Drop 'hardly'.

question: In my opinion a pencil is always more preferable to a pen.
explanation: Drop 'more'.

question: The salesman tried to mislead me with a talk of amazing savings on heating bills.
options: with a talk of amazing savings on heating bills.
explanation: No grammatical error in the sentence.

question: He is well up these days despite having ill health
explanation: Use 'off' for 'up'.

question: He regarded his marriage as a mean to an end; he just wanted his wife's wealth.
options: as a mean to an end;
he just wanted his wife's wealth.
correctAnswer: as a mean to an end;
explanation: Use 'means' for 'mean'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: To be intelligent is more essential than being hard working.
Being intelligent is more important than to be hard working.
For one to be intelligent is more important than being hard working.
Being intelligent is more essential than being hard working.
correctAnswer: Being intelligent is more essential than being hard working.
explanation: Both halves of a comparison must take the same form, so 'Being intelligent' pairs with 'being hard working'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: If he wins the prize I would be very happy.
If he were to win the prize I'll be very happy.
If he was to win the prize I would be very happy.
If he were to win the prize I would be very happy.
correctAnswer: If he were to win the prize I would be very happy.
explanation: An improbable condition takes 'were to' in the if-clause and 'would' in the main clause.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Our school had won the match if only we have concentrated.
Our school would have won the match if only we would have concentrated.
Our school would have won the match if only we had concentrated.
Our school had won the match if only we would have concentrated.
correctAnswer: Our school would have won the match if only we had concentrated.
explanation: An unfulfilled past condition takes the past perfect in the if-clause and 'would have + past participle' in the main clause.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: My sister had left for America last week.
My sister has been left for America last week.
My sister has left for America last week.
My sister left for America last week.
correctAnswer: My sister left for America last week.
explanation: 'Last week' is a finished past time, so the simple past is required rather than any perfect tense.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: It is high time he will start earning.
It is high time he started earning.
It is high time he starts earning.
It is high time he has started earning.
correctAnswer: It is high time he started earning.
explanation: After 'It is high time', the verb goes into the past subjunctive.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: It is a pleasure to see an alligator basking in the sunshine on a river bank as long as ninety feet.
It is a pleasure to see an alligator as long as ninety feet basking in the sunshine on a river bank.
It is a pleasure to see an alligator basking in the sunshine as long as ninety feet on a river bank.
It is a pleasure to see an alligator basking as long as ninety feet in the sunshine on a river bank.
correctAnswer: It is a pleasure to see an alligator as long as ninety feet basking in the sunshine on a river bank.
explanation: 'As long as ninety feet' describes the alligator, so it must stand next to that noun.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The villagers were enjoying winter evening around the fire.
The villagers were enjoying winter evening around a fire.
The villagers were enjoying winter evening around fire.
The villagers were enjoying winter evening round fire.
correctAnswer: The villagers were enjoying winter evening around the fire.
explanation: The villagers sat around one particular fire, so the definite article 'the' is needed.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: When he had lost the book he searched it everywhere.
When he lost the book he searched for it everywhere.
When he lost the book he had searched for it everywhere.
When he lost the book he searched it up everywhere.
correctAnswer: When he lost the book he searched for it everywhere.
explanation: 'Search for' is used when you are looking for something; 'search' alone means to examine a place or a person.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: This was the ideal book available in the market.
This was most ideal book available in the market.
This was a most ideal book available in the market.
This was the most ideal book available in the market.
correctAnswer: This was the ideal book available in the market.
explanation: 'Ideal' is an absolute adjective and cannot be graded with 'most'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: An one-eyed person was seen roaming about the streets.
A one-eyed person was seen roaming about the streets.
The one-eyed person was seen roaming about the streets.
One-eyed person was seen roaming about the streets.
correctAnswer: A one-eyed person was seen roaming about the streets.
explanation: 'One' begins with a consonant sound, so it takes 'a' and not 'an'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: It is the duty of a house-wife to wait on the guest.
It is the duty of a house-wife to wait for the guest.
It is the duty of a house-wife to wait the guest.
It is the duty of a house-wife to await the guest.
correctAnswer: It is the duty of a house-wife to wait on the guest.
explanation: 'Wait on' means to serve or attend to someone, which is the sense required here.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: You are not working hard so your success is out of a question.
You are not working hard so your success is out of the question.
You are not working hard so your success is out of question.
You are not working hard so your success is not out of the question.
correctAnswer: You are not working hard so your success is out of the question.
explanation: 'Out of the question' is the fixed idiom meaning impossible.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: You cannot win my confidence without ever believing me.
You cannot win my confidence without never believing me.
You cannot win my confidence without not believing me.
You cannot win my confidence with ever believing me.
correctAnswer: You cannot win my confidence without ever believing me.
explanation: 'Without' is already negative, so no second negative may follow it.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: It is strange that you don't know swimming.
It is strange that you don't know how to swim.
It is strange that you don't know how to swimming.
It is strange that you don't know to swim.
correctAnswer: It is strange that you don't know how to swim.
explanation: When it refers to a skill, 'know' takes 'how to' followed by the base verb.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The receptionist must answer courteously the questions what are asked by the callers.
The receptionist must answer courteously the questions of all the callers.
The receptionist should answer courteously the questions of all the callers.
The receptionist courteously should answer the question of callers.
correctAnswer: The receptionist should answer courteously the questions of all the callers.
explanation: 'Should' expresses the expected duty, and 'the questions of all the callers' avoids the wrong relative 'what'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: As he was sick, he was quite enthusiastic.
Since he was sick, he was quite enthusiastic.
As sick he was, he was quite enthusiastic.
Sick as he was, he was quite enthusiastic.
correctAnswer: Sick as he was, he was quite enthusiastic.
explanation: This concessive pattern puts the adjective first: adjective + as + subject + verb.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Both my brother and my sister love me but I should say that she loves me more than he.
Both my brother and my sister love me but I should say that she loves more than him.
Both my brother and my sister love me but I should say that she loves me more than him.
Both my brother and my sister love me but I should say that she loves I more than he.
correctAnswer: Both my brother and my sister love me but I should say that she loves me more than he.
explanation: The comparison is between two subjects, so the nominative 'he' is required — she loves me more than he does.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: I am an optimist and therefore I generally differ with you.
I am an optimist and therefore I generally differ from you.
I am an optimist and therefore I generally differ in you.
I am an optimist and therefore I generally differ you.
correctAnswer: I am an optimist and therefore I generally differ with you.
explanation: You differ with a person when you disagree; 'differ from' means to be unlike.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Neena can do it alone and no body else can do it.
Neena can do it and nobody else can do it.
Neena alone can do it and nobody else can do it.
Alone Neena can do it and no body else can do it.
correctAnswer: Neena can do it and nobody else can do it.
explanation: 'Alone' becomes redundant once 'nobody else' has been said.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Due to want of rain the wells have gone dry.
Because of want of rain the wells have gone dry.
For want of rain the wells have gone dry.
Owing to want of rain the wells have gone dry.
correctAnswer: For want of rain the wells have gone dry.
explanation: 'For want of' is the idiom meaning 'because of a lack of'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: As the train which was my usual was missing I had to travel.
Having missed the train which I usually catch and had to travel.
I missed the train which I usually catch and had to travel by the next.
I missed not only the train which I usually catch but had to travel on the next.
correctAnswer: I missed the train which I usually catch and had to travel by the next.
explanation: Both verbs need the same subject, and 'travel by the next' is the natural idiom.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He may be poor now but he appears to have been rich in his youth.
He may be poor now but he appears to be rich in his youth.
He may be poor now but he appears being rich in his youth.
He may be poor now but he appears to rich in his youth.
correctAnswer: He may be poor now but he appears to have been rich in his youth.
explanation: The perfect infinitive 'to have been' places the wealth earlier in time than 'appears'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He went to the wholesale market and bought the cheap rations.
He went to the wholesale market and bought the rations cheap.
He went to the wholesale market and bought rations cheaply.
He went to the wholesale market and cheaply bought rations.
correctAnswer: He went to the wholesale market and bought the rations cheap.
explanation: 'Buy cheap' is a fixed expression in which 'cheap' works adverbially.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: I went yesterday to the bank to collect the pass book.
I went to the bank to collect the pass book.
Yesterday to collect the pass book I went to the bank.
To collect the pass book yesterday I went to the bank.
correctAnswer: I went yesterday to the bank to collect the pass book.
explanation: The sentence keeps its natural order with the time adverb next to the verb; the other versions invert it awkwardly.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The principal appointed him as a peon in the college.
The principal appointed him a peon in the college.
As a peon the Principal appointed him in the college.
The principal as a peon appointed him in the college.
correctAnswer: The principal appointed him a peon in the college.
explanation: 'Appoint' takes a direct object and a complement without 'as'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The team is confident to win the match.
The team is confident of winning the match.
The team is confident of win the match.
The team is confident for winning the match.
correctAnswer: The team is confident of winning the match.
explanation: 'Confident' is followed by 'of' and then a gerund.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He is one of the best policeman who has ever lived.
He is one of the best policeman who have ever lived.
He is one of the best policemen that have ever lived.
He is one of the best policeman that has ever lived.
correctAnswer: He is one of the best policemen that have ever lived.
explanation: 'One of the best' takes a plural noun, and the relative clause agrees with that plural.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: My sister is the poet and the philosopher.
My sister is a poet and the philosopher.
My sister is a poet and a philosopher.
My sister is a poet and philosopher.
correctAnswer: My sister is a poet and philosopher.
explanation: One article is enough because both nouns describe the same person.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Meena seldom or ever refuses an invitation.
Meena seldom or always refuses an invitation.
Meena seldom or never refuses an invitation.
Meena seldom if never refuses an invitation.
correctAnswer: Meena seldom or never refuses an invitation.
explanation: 'Seldom or never' is the established idiom.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: There is no meaning in what you say.
There is no meaning in that you say.
There is no meaning as to what you say.
There is no meaning that you say.
correctAnswer: There is no meaning in what you say.
explanation: After the preposition 'in', 'what' serves as the relative pronoun meaning 'the thing that'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: I hope you will excuse my leaving early.
I hope you will excuse me leaving early.
I hope you will excuse mine leaving early.
I hope you will excuse leaving early.
correctAnswer: I hope you will excuse my leaving early.
explanation: A gerund after 'excuse' takes a possessive adjective, not an object pronoun.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: I am ready to say this at her face.
I am ready to say this on her face.
I am ready to say this in her face.
I am ready to say this to her face.
correctAnswer: I am ready to say this to her face.
explanation: 'To one's face' is the idiom for saying something openly to somebody.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: On account of shortage of time both of them cannot finish their work.
On account of shortage of time none of them can finish their work.
On account of shortage of time neither of them can finish his work.
On account of shortage of time neither of them cannot finish his work.
correctAnswer: On account of shortage of time neither of them can finish his work.
explanation: 'Neither' is singular, so it takes a singular verb and a singular pronoun, and it already carries the negative.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Many problems are staring at my face.
Many problems are staring in my face.
Many problems are staring me into my face.
Many problems are staring me in my face.
correctAnswer: Many problems are staring me in my face.
explanation: 'Stare somebody in the face' keeps the person as the object of the verb.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The cow does not eat anything else. It lives on grass and leaves.
The cow does not eat anything else. It lives at grass and leaves.
The cow does not eat anything else. It lives in grass and leaves.
The cow does not eat anything else. It lives for grass and leaves.
correctAnswer: The cow does not eat anything else. It lives on grass and leaves.
explanation: 'Live on' is the idiom for the food a creature subsists on.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: As one of his arms was amputated on account of an accident, the company will compensate the loss to him.
As one of his arms was amputated on account of an accident, the company will compensate him for the loss.
As one of his arms was amputated on account of an accident, the company will compensate him in the loss.
As one of his arms was amputated on account of an accident, the company will compensate his loss.
correctAnswer: As one of his arms was amputated on account of an accident, the company will compensate him for the loss.
explanation: 'Compensate' takes the person as its object, followed by 'for' the thing lost.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Now I have cancelled my meeting though I was to go there.
Now I have cancelled my meeting though I have to go there.
Now I have cancelled my meeting though I am to go there.
Now I have cancelled my meeting though I was to have gone there.
correctAnswer: Now I have cancelled my meeting though I was to have gone there.
explanation: 'Was to have gone' shows an arrangement that was never carried out.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: She insisted on me to stay there.
She insisted on me staying there.
She insisted on my staying there.
She insisted in my staying there.
correctAnswer: She insisted on my staying there.
explanation: 'Insist on' is followed by a gerund with a possessive adjective.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: You can meet my father only when he goes to prison.
You can meet father only when he goes into prison.
You can meet my father only when he goes in prison.
You can meet my father only when he goes to the prison.
correctAnswer: You can meet my father only when he goes to the prison.
explanation: 'Go to the prison' means visiting the building, whereas 'go to prison' would mean being imprisoned.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Since the dividend being declared then the notices were prepared for mailing.
No sooner had the dividend being declared then the notices were prepared for mailing.
No sooner had the dividend been declared than the notices were prepared for mailing.
Scarcely had the dividend being declared than the notices were sent out.
correctAnswer: No sooner had the dividend been declared than the notices were prepared for mailing.
explanation: 'No sooner' inverts the auxiliary and pairs with 'than', and the passive needs 'been declared'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He did not report for work today. He must has gone to the party.
He did not report for work today. He must have gone to the party.
He did not report for work today. He must go to the party.
He did not report for work today. He must had gone to the party.
correctAnswer: He did not report for work today. He must have gone to the party.
explanation: A deduction about the past takes 'must have' with the past participle.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: She is not as wise as his brother.
She is not equally wise as his brother.
She is not as wise like his brother.
She is not so wise as his brother.
correctAnswer: She is not so wise as his brother.
explanation: In a negative comparison, 'so ... as' is preferred to 'as ... as'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: There will be a meeting in the long room at 4 o'clock of all the boys who play cricket and football.
There will be in the long room at 4 o'clock a meeting of all the boys who play cricket and football.
In the long room at 4 o'clock there will be a meeting of all the boys who play cricket and football.
There will be a meeting of all the boys who play cricket and football at 4 o'clock.
correctAnswer: In the long room at 4 o'clock there will be a meeting of all the boys who play cricket and football.
explanation: Placing the adverbials first keeps 'a meeting of all the boys' together and removes the ambiguity.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The teacher made it a point to explain him the situation.
The teacher made it a point to explain the situation him.
The teacher made it a point explain him about the situation.
The teacher made it a point to explain the situation to him.
correctAnswer: The teacher made it a point to explain the situation to him.
explanation: 'Explain' takes the thing explained as its object and the person after 'to'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The landlady made the servant to run to market to fetch her sweets.
The landlady made the servant run to market to fetch her sweets.
The landlady made to the servant to run to market to fetch her sweets.
The landlady made to the servant run to market to fetch her sweets.
correctAnswer: The landlady made the servant run to market to fetch her sweets.
explanation: After the causative 'make', the bare infinitive is used.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The audience looked at him while he spoke.
The audience looked at him while he had spoken.
The audience looked at him while he was speaking.
The audience looked at him while he had been speaking.
correctAnswer: The audience looked at him while he was speaking.
explanation: 'While' introduces an action in progress, which calls for the past continuous.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Your answers are better than Mohan.
Your answers are better than Mohan's.
Your answers are better than those of Mohan's.
Your answers are better than answered by Mohan.
correctAnswer: Your answers are better than Mohan's.
explanation: Answers are being compared with answers, so the possessive 'Mohan's' is required.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Everybody knows that Rahul is nothing else but a cheat.
Everybody knows that Rahul is nothing else than a cheat.
Everybody knows that Rahul is nothing else except a cheat.
Everybody knows that Rahul is nothing but for a cheat.
correctAnswer: Everybody knows that Rahul is nothing else but a cheat.
explanation: 'Nothing else but' is the fixed idiom.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The manager asked him how he would avail this opportunity.
The manager asked him how he would avail of this opportunity.
The manager asked him how he would avail himself of this opportunity.
The manager asked him how he would avail himself this opportunity.
correctAnswer: The manager asked him how he would avail himself of this opportunity.
explanation: 'Avail' is used reflexively and followed by 'of'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The teacher asked the students to thoroughly study this book.
The teacher asked the students thoroughly to study this book.
The teacher asked thoroughly the students to study this book.
The teacher asked the students to study thoroughly this book.
correctAnswer: The teacher asked the students to study thoroughly this book.
explanation: The adverb follows the verb it modifies instead of splitting the infinitive.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The important lessons are as following.
The important lessons are as follows.
The important lessons are as follow.
correctAnswer: The important lessons are as follows.
explanation: 'As follows' never changes its form, however many items are listed.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The teacher asked the student with a frown on his face to leave the room.
The teacher asked with a frown on his face the student to leave the room.
With a frown on his face the teacher asked the student to leave the room.
The teacher asked the student to leave the room with a frown on his face.
correctAnswer: With a frown on his face the teacher asked the student to leave the room.
explanation: The frown belongs to the teacher, so the phrase must stand next to 'the teacher'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The typists had corrected the errors had they known that the supervisors would have seen the report.
The supervisors reprimanded the typists whom they believed had made careless errors.
The errors in the typed reports were so numerous that they could hardly be overlooked.
The typist would have corrected the errors had they known that the supervisor would see the reports.
correctAnswer: The errors in the typed reports were so numerous that they could hardly be overlooked.
explanation: The 'so ... that' construction is complete here, while the other options misuse the conditional or the relative pronoun.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He carried the little child and me on his shoulders.
It was me that gave away the prizes.
All what he said had no effect on me.
They who did this thing should be punished.
correctAnswer: He carried the little child and me on his shoulders.
explanation: As the object of 'carried', the pronoun takes its objective form 'me'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: In order to solve the murder case a C.B.I. officer is looking about the matter.
It is high time that you went to bed.
Though he looked innocent he turned into be cheat.
The majority of the workers was divided on the issue.
correctAnswer: It is high time that you went to bed.
explanation: After 'It is high time', the past subjunctive 'went' is used.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: You cannot win my confidence until you are sincere.
When he lost the book he searched it everywhere.
She was intent to harm her friends.
I have not met my friend for the last five days.
correctAnswer: I have not met my friend for the last five days.
explanation: A period running up to the present takes the present perfect with 'for'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He started to work hard lest he might starve in old age.
He started working hard lest he should not starve in old age.
He started to work hard lest he should starve in old age.
He started working hard lest he should starve in old age.
correctAnswer: He started working hard lest he should starve in old age.
explanation: 'Lest' already carries the negative and is followed by 'should'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: If I had money I would have bought the new house tomorrow.
If I had had money I would have bought a new house tomorrow.
If I had had money I would buy a new house tomorrow.
If I had money I would buy a new house tomorrow.
correctAnswer: If I had money I would buy a new house tomorrow.
explanation: An unreal present condition takes the past tense with 'would' and the base verb.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Taking my food I left for college.
While I was taking my food I left for college.
Having taken my food I left for college.
Taking my food I shall leave for college.
correctAnswer: Having taken my food I left for college.
explanation: The perfect participle 'having taken' shows the meal was finished before he left.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The harassed wife shot herself after bidding her husband the last good bye with a gun.
The harassed wife with a gun shot herself after bidding her husband the last good bye.
The harassed wife shot herself with a gun after bidding her husband the last good bye.
With a gun the harassed wife shot herself after bidding her husband the last good bye.
correctAnswer: The harassed wife shot herself with a gun after bidding her husband the last good bye.
explanation: 'With a gun' modifies 'shot', so it must stand beside that verb.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He repeated the essay word by word.
Being a rainy day he did not go out.
She is senior but not more efficient than I.
All his friends are very sincere.
correctAnswer: All his friends are very sincere.
explanation: Only this option is free of error: 'word by word' should be 'word for word', 'Being a rainy day' dangles, and 'senior' takes 'to' rather than 'than'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: She had waited long before her husband had returned.
She waited long when her husband returned.
She had waited long after her husband returned.
She had waited long before her husband returned.
correctAnswer: She had waited long before her husband returned.
explanation: The earlier action takes the past perfect and the later one the simple past.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Even if intelligent he may be he can't succeed.
If intelligent he may be he can't succeed.
However intelligent he may be he can't succeed.
Even intelligent he may be he can't pass.
correctAnswer: However intelligent he may be he can't succeed.
explanation: 'However' followed by the adjective is the correct concessive form.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Had I been you I would help him.
If I had been you I would help him.
Should I you I would help him.
Were I you I would help him.
correctAnswer: Were I you I would help him.
explanation: The subjunctive 'were' with inversion states an unreal present condition.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: I realised later on that he cheated me.
I had realised later that he cheated me.
I had realised later that he had cheated me.
I realised later on that he had cheated me.
correctAnswer: I realised later on that he had cheated me.
explanation: The cheating happened before the realisation, so it takes the past perfect.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: They arrived early because they may not miss the train.
They arrived early that they may not miss the train.
They arrived early when they miss the train.
They arrived early so that they might not miss the train.
correctAnswer: They arrived early so that they might not miss the train.
explanation: A purpose clause after a past main verb takes 'so that' with 'might'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: I was rather impressed by the manner of the speaker than by his matter.
I was impressed by the manner of the speaker rather than by his matter.
Rather I was impressed by the manner of the speaker than by his matter.
I was impressed rather by the manner of the speaker than by his matter.
correctAnswer: I was impressed rather by the manner of the speaker than by his matter.
explanation: 'Rather' stands immediately before the phrase that 'than' contrasts it with.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He is vain as though he were a millionaire.
She acted as if her mother asked her to do.
She carried the child carefully lest it should not fall.
I don't relish the food whose taste is sour.
correctAnswer: He is vain as though he were a millionaire.
explanation: 'As though' introduces an unreal comparison and takes the subjunctive 'were'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The nature of my brother is the same as yours.
This is one of those novels which is admired all over the world.
He is such a friend that will sacrifice for me.
correctAnswer: The nature of my brother is the same as yours.
explanation: 'The same as' is the correct pairing for this comparison.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: So quickly he returned from market that I was surprised.
So quickly did he returned from the market that I was surprised.
So quickly did he return from the market that I was surprised.
So quickly did he return from the market that I had been surprised.
correctAnswer: So quickly did he return from the market that I was surprised.
explanation: When 'so + adverb' opens the sentence, the auxiliary is inverted and the main verb stays in its base form.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Would you help my brother I shall get you a decent job.
Had you helped my brother I shall get you a decent job.
Did you help my brother I shall get you a decent job.
Should you help my brother I'll get you a decent job.
correctAnswer: Should you help my brother I'll get you a decent job.
explanation: 'Should' with inversion expresses an open condition about the future.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: A summon has been served on him.
A summons have been served on him.
A summons has been served on him.
A summon have been served to him.
correctAnswer: A summons has been served on him.
explanation: 'Summons' in this legal sense is singular and takes a singular verb.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: You are not allowed to enter into the house.
You are not allowed to enter the house.
You are not allowed to enter in the house.
You are not allowed to enter on the house.
correctAnswer: You are not allowed to enter the house.
explanation: 'Enter' is transitive and needs no preposition after it.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Little care was needed to avert the accident.
The little care was needed to avert the accident.
A little care was needed to avert the accident.
Less care was needed to avert the accident.
correctAnswer: A little care was needed to avert the accident.
explanation: 'A little' means some, the positive sense needed here; 'little' alone would mean hardly any.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Could you please help me with any money?
Could you please help me with some money?
Would you please help me with any money?
Can you please help me with some money?
correctAnswer: Could you please help me with some money?
explanation: A polite request takes 'some' rather than 'any'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Leena is a most intelligent student in the class.
Leena is the most intelligent student.
Leena is a most intelligent student.
Leena is most intelligent student in the class.
correctAnswer: Leena is a most intelligent student.
explanation: 'A most' means 'very'; adding 'in the class' would call for the superlative 'the most'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: She is more intelligent than any other boy in the class.
She is more intelligent than any girl in the class.
She is more intelligent than any other girl in the class.
She is the most intelligent than any other girl in the class.
correctAnswer: She is more intelligent than any other girl in the class.
explanation: Comparing a girl with the rest of her own group requires 'any other'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The teaching staff must take their lectures regularly when are asked by the Principal.
The teaching staff would have taken lectures regularly had they known that the Principal would know about it.
The teaching staff had taken the lectures regularly had they known that the Principal would come to know about it.
Many irregularities were found in their lectures by the Principal and he could not be disregarded them.
correctAnswer: The teaching staff would have taken lectures regularly had they known that the Principal would know about it.
explanation: The unreal past condition takes 'had known' with 'would have taken'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Anita was sitting with her husband on the steps of the temple with her lap full of newspapers when Bunty and Bitto came up.
Anita with her lap full of newspapers was sitting with her husband on the steps of the temple when Bunty and Bitto came up.
With her lap full of newspapers Anita was sitting with her husband on the steps of the temple when Bunty and Bitto came up.
Anita was sitting with her husband on the steps of the temple when Bunty and Bittu came up with her lap full of newspapers.
correctAnswer: Anita with her lap full of newspapers was sitting with her husband on the steps of the temple when Bunty and Bitto came up.
explanation: The lap full of newspapers is Anita's, so the phrase must stand next to her name.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: As he is careless he will not hear what the teacher says.
As he is careless he will not hear to what the teacher says.
As he is careless he will not listen what the teacher says.
As he is careless he will not listen to what the teacher says.
correctAnswer: As he is careless he will not listen to what the teacher says.
explanation: 'Listen' means to pay attention and is followed by 'to'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Shikha has been known by me for five years.
Shikha is known by me for five years.
Shikha is known to me for five years.
Shikha has been known to me for five years.
correctAnswer: Shikha has been known to me for five years.
explanation: A state continuing over a period takes the present perfect, and one is known 'to' a person.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: As soon as holidays be begin than this beach will become very crowded.
Since the holidays being started this beach becomes very crowded.
As soon as the holidays begin, this beach becomes very crowded.
No sooner did the holiday begin than this beach will become very crowded.
correctAnswer: As soon as the holidays begin, this beach becomes very crowded.
explanation: A general truth takes the simple present in both clauses.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: You must aspire for the post according to your capability.
You must aspire to the post according to your capability.
You must aspire after the post according to your capability.
You must aspire the post according to your capability.
correctAnswer: You must aspire to the post according to your capability.
explanation: 'Aspire' takes 'to' before the thing desired.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: A good teacher provides a student all the useful information.
A good teacher provides to a student all the useful information.
A good teacher provides a student with all the useful information.
A good teacher provides to student with all the useful information.
correctAnswer: A good teacher provides a student with all the useful information.
explanation: The pattern is 'provide somebody with something'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Nobody will want to play in his team if he does not treat people kindly.
If he will not treat people kindly nobody will want to play in his team.
Nobody will treat people kindly if he does not want to play in his team.
Nobody will want to treat people if he does not play in his team kindly.
correctAnswer: Nobody will want to play in his team if he does not treat people kindly.
explanation: The if-clause takes the simple present while the main clause takes the future.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The priest read to the dying man couplets from the scriptures.
The priest read the dying man the couplets from the scriptures.
The priest read for the dying man the couplets from the scriptures.
The priest read the couplets from the scriptures for the dying man.
correctAnswer: The priest read the dying man the couplets from the scriptures.
explanation: 'Read' can take the indirect object before the direct object without a preposition.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: I do not understand to whom she is talking.
I do not understand whom she is talking about.
I do not understand who she is talking to.
I do not understand whom she is talking.
correctAnswer: I do not understand who she is talking to.
explanation: 'Talk' needs its preposition 'to', which is kept at the end of the clause.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The boy regretted that with a plastered leg he had spent a greater part of his vacation in the chair.
The boy regretted that he had spent a greater part of his vacation in the chair with a plastered leg.
With a plastered leg, the boy regretted that he had spent a greater part of his vacation in the chair.
The boy with a plastered leg regretted that he had spent a greater part of his vacation in the chair.
correctAnswer: The boy with a plastered leg regretted that he had spent a greater part of his vacation in the chair.
explanation: The plastered leg belongs to the boy, so the phrase must stand next to 'the boy'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: In thirty-seven bomb blasts, fortunately only five lives were lost.
In thirty-seven bomb blasts, only five lives were fortunately lost.
In fortunately thirty-seven bomb blasts only five lives were lost.
Fortunately, in thirty-seven bomb blasts, only five lives were lost.
correctAnswer: Fortunately, in thirty-seven bomb blasts, only five lives were lost.
explanation: 'Fortunately' comments on the whole sentence, so it belongs at the beginning.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: She is annoyed with you. You ought not to tell her secrets to her mother.
She is annoyed with you. You ought not to have told her secrets to her mother.
She is annoyed with you, you ought to tell her secrets to her mother.
She is annoyed with you. You ought to have told her secrets to her mother.
correctAnswer: She is annoyed with you. You ought not to have told her secrets to her mother.
explanation: 'Ought not to have told' expresses a past action that should not have happened.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: It is the best which she could do for me.
It is the best what she could do for me.
It is the best that she could do for me.
It is best that she could for me.
correctAnswer: It is the best that she could do for me.
explanation: After a superlative, the relative pronoun used is 'that'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The early age of three or four years, would begin our first recollection of the world, for many of us.
Our first recollection of the world, for many of us, would be early age of three or four years.
For many of us, our first recollection of the world is from the early age of only three or four years.
For many of us, our first recollection of the world has been the early age of only three or four years.
correctAnswer: For many of us, our first recollection of the world is from the early age of only three or four years.
explanation: A recollection dates 'from' an age, and this version keeps the subject and verb in agreement.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Now-a-days singing is a very profitable profession.
Now-a-days the singing is a very profitable profession.
Now-a-days singing is very profitable profession.
Now-a-days the singing is very profitable profession.
correctAnswer: Now-a-days singing is a very profitable profession.
explanation: A gerund used in a general sense takes no article, while the countable 'profession' takes 'a'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: The report was useless to them because there was no needed information.
Since the report lacked needed information would have not been useful to them.
Since the report did not control the needed information it was not really useful to them.
Since the report lacked the needed information it was of no use to them.
correctAnswer: Since the report lacked the needed information it was of no use to them.
explanation: After the 'Since' clause, the main clause still needs its own subject and verb — 'it was of no use to them'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Men are rather impressed by beauty than by character.
Men are impressed rather by beauty than by character.
Rather men are impressed by beauty than by character.
Men are impressed by beauty than by character.
correctAnswer: Men are impressed rather by beauty than by character.
explanation: 'Rather' stands directly before the phrase that 'than' contrasts it with.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: So quickly she ran upstairs that she over took me.
So quickly did she ran upstairs that she over took me.
She ran so quickly upstairs that she had overtaken me.
So quickly did she run upstairs that she overtook me.
correctAnswer: So quickly did she run upstairs that she overtook me.
explanation: The inversion after 'so quickly' leaves the main verb in its base form 'run'.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: He wasn't rich by any means, although he never turned down anyone who needed help.
Being not rich by any means he never turned away, anyone who needed help.
He wasn't rich by any means but he never turned away anyone who needed help.
Since he wasn't rich by any means, he never turned away anyone who needed help.
correctAnswer: He wasn't rich by any means but he never turned away anyone who needed help.
explanation: The two clauses contrast, so 'but' is the right connective and 'turn away' the right phrasal verb.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Some people consider Karan the valorous hero of all the characters in the Mahabharata.
Some people consider Karan as the most valorous hero of all the characters in the Mahabharata.
Some people consider Karan the most valorous hero of all the other characters in the Mahabharata.
Some people consider Karan the most valorous hero of all the characters in the Mahabharata.
correctAnswer: Some people consider Karan the most valorous hero of all the characters in the Mahabharata.
explanation: 'Consider' takes no 'as', and the superlative already covers all the characters.

question: Select the most suitable sentence in respect of meaning and grammatical correctness.
options: Neither she comes nor she writes.
Neither does she comes nor she writes.
Neither does she come nor writes.
Neither does she come nor does she write.
correctAnswer: Neither does she come nor does she write.
explanation: 'Neither ... nor' at the head of a sentence requires inversion in both halves.
